snippet.title: The History of Ceramics Podcast: How Ceramics became Funk Art
snippet.description:
Join Stephanie Rozene and guest Garth Johnson as they travel to the West Coast  of America in the year 1967 when a show named Funk would change ceramics for ever.

Join Stephanie Rozene and guest Garth Johnson as they travel to the West Coast of America in 1967 when a show named Funk would showcase ceramics as a provokative art form. Using humour, satire, colour and shock these Funk artists critiqued the world around them and changed ceramics forever.  No longer utiliatarian vessels - this was art that shocked.

Featured Artworks:

Robert Arneson Images 
01. Banded White Bottle, 1958, glazed stoneware, ceramic, 13 1/2 x 5 inches, Collection of Weisman Art Museum 

02. No Deposit, No Return 1961 glazed stoneware 10 3/4 x 5 x 5 inches[Text Wrapping Break] Los Angeles County Museum of Art, Smits Ceramic Purchase Fund, Modern Art Deaccession Fund, and the Decorative Arts Council. Collection of Los Angeles County Museum of Art. 

03. Jack and John Trophy 1964  glazed earthenware, ceramic 31 1/2 x 14 x 8 inches Private Collection 

04. 3 Spouted Footed Vase 1959 ceramic 10 1/2 x 9 1/2 x 6 1/2 inches 

05. His and Her’s 1964  ceramic  34 x 24 x 28 inches Collection of Iris & B. Gerald Cantor Center for Visual Arts, Stanford University 

06. Typewriter #1 (Touch System) 1965 earthenware, ceramic, and nail polish[Text Wrapping Break] 6 x 11 1/2 x 12 1/2 inches University of California, Berkeley Art Museum 

07.John with Art 1964  glazed ceramic 36 x 37 1/2 x 47 inches Collection of Seattle Art Museum 

08. Self Portrait of the Artists Losing His Marbles 1965 glazed ceramic 31 x 17 1/2 x 9 1/2 inches Collection of Museum of Arts and Design, New York 

09. Alice House Wall 1967 glazed cerami  71 x 93 x 15 1/4 inches  Collection of Museum of Arts and Design, New York 

10. Assassination of a Famous Nut Artist 1971 underglazed and glazed earthenware[Text Wrapping Break] 30 x 22 x 13 inches Collection of the Iris and B. Gerald Cantor Center for the Visual Arts at Stanford University 

11. California Artist 1983  polychrome and patinaed bronze edition of 3, 1 A.P. with bronze base 78 x 29 x 23 1/2 inches 

12. Portrait of George 1981  glazed ceramic 94 x 31 1/2 x 31 1/4 inches Collection of San Francisco Museum of Modern Art 

13. George Moscone 1981 conte, oil pastel, acrylic on paper 52 1/2 x 42 inches[Text Wrapping Break] Collection of University of California, Berkeley Art Museum 

14. General Nuke 1985 ceramic, bronze (unique), granite 74 1/4 x 32 1/2 x 37 inches[Text Wrapping Break] Collection of Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden 

Other Images 

15. Peter Saul “Relax in Electric Chair (Dirty Guy),” 1965, styrofoam, fiberglass, and plastic enamel, 55 x 24 x 24 in 

16Peter Voulkos, Rocking Pot, 1956, stoneware with colemanite wash, 13 5⁄8 x 21 x 17 1⁄2 in. (34.6 x 53.3 x 44.6 cm.), Smithsonian American Art Museum, Gift of the James Renwick Alliance and various donors and museum purchase, 1983.79 

17 Peter Voulkos, Hole in One, 1978, ceramic, 43 1⁄2 x 16 1⁄2 in. (110.5 x 41.9 cm) diam., Smithsonian American Art Museum, Bequest of Edith S. and Arthur J. Levin, 2005.5.73, © 1978, Voulkos Family Trust  

18. Bottle, circa 1955. Antonio Prieto (American, born Spain, 1912–1967) Stoneware, reduction fired with sgraffito decoration, 13-3/4 in. x 7-1/4 in. (diam.), Crocker Art Museum, gift of the Artist, 1959.2 

19. Arneson at TB-9, Davis, CA 1991 Photo Credit: James Woodson 

20. David Gilhooley, Frog Sandwich (From the Frog Series), Glazed Earthenware 12x13x13cm, 1976. 

Clayton Bailey Images 
21. Clayton Bailey with Jughead Pots 

22.  Clayton Bailey CRITTER STOOL- 1963 Salt Glazed Stoneware 20" X 20" x 20" 

23 Clayton Bailey CRITTER RIDER- 1960 Stoneware 18" X 12' X 10" 

24 Clayton Bailey with Jugheads pots 

25 Garth Johnson as the Curator of Kaolithic Curiosities, 2021 

26. Garth Johnson as the Curator of Kaolithic Curiosities sitting in Clayton Bailey’s Stool, 2021 

25 Clayton Bailey, Nose Cup 1968. Earthenware with commercial glazes and luster. Collection of Garth Johnson (permission to publish) 

26 Clayton Bailey Nite Pots -KISSING POTS - 1965 Painted Earthenware

snippet.title: Gordon Ramsay's American Food Adventure | America 250 Special | Uncharted MEGA Episode | Nat Geo
snippet.description:
Celebrate America's 250th anniversary with Gordon Ramsay and National Geographic and explore the people, landscapes, and regional food traditions that help define the United States. In this 2+ hour Gordon Ramsay: Uncharted Mega Episode, Gordon travels from Louisiana's bayous to the Great Smoky Mountains and the rugged landscapes of Texas in search of authentic American cuisine, local ingredients, and unforgettable culinary traditions. He experiences a crawfish boil, rappels down a waterfall to fish for trout, and crafts his own spin on Texas barbecue. Featuring three, full episodes: 

Louisiana's Bayou Cuisine - 00:00 
When Chef Ramsay is told that “Cajun comes from the soul,” his soul searching takes him to South Louisiana’s swamps to test his skills and his luck.

The Great Smoky Mountains - 44:02 
Gordon rappels, kayaks, and forages his way through the Smoky Mountains in a hunt for some of the most unique ingredients the region has to offer. 

Texas Throwdown - 01:28:04
Chef Ramsay learns the meaning of “Texas Tough” as he herds cattle, catches a rattlesnake and hunts feral hog in the Lone Star State.

snippet.title: 7 IMPOSSIBLE Ancient Discoveries We Still Can’t Explain
snippet.description:
How did a piece of Ancient Rome end up buried in a Mexican grave more than a thousand years before the first European ships were supposed to arrive? Across the ancient world, there are monuments, artifacts, and events that were documented, studied, and then left without answers — not because they were fake, but because they do not fit the timeline we rely on.

How do enormous figures appear with no clear method of construction? Why do entire cultures leave behind traces that end suddenly and violently, with no clear explanation? And why do certain sites continue to spark debate decades after their discovery, with no consensus in sight?

In this feature-length documentary, we investigate a collection of real ancient mysteries rooted in archaeology, lost civilizations, and unexplained historical events. Each case is supported by physical evidence and historical records, yet remains unresolved. These are not myths or legends — they are documented discoveries that still challenge historians, archaeologists, and researchers today.

snippet.title: We Simulated A Scuba Dive To Titanic: It Is Terrifying
snippet.description:
At 12,500 feet below the surface, the ocean pressure is roughly 400 times greater than at sea level. In this Disaster Documentary, we explore the terrifying "what if" scenario of a human diver attempting to reach the crow's nest of the RMS Titanic. 

Using advanced physics simulations and hyper-realistic underwater rendering, we break down exactly what would happen to a scuba diver attempting to navigate the rusted ruins of the famous ocean liner.  This is a story that sounds like fiction, but it is grounded in terrifying science. 

Discover the chilling reality of deep-sea pressure, the limitations of atmospheric diving suits, and the haunting isolation of exploring the ultimate ghost ship without the protection of a submarine. We analyze the raw power of the elements and the biological limits of the human body.  

If extreme deep-sea diving suits advance enough in our lifetime, would you ever dare to visit the crow's nest yourself? Let us know in the comments below.

snippet.title: Barbarossa: The Day Hitler Underestimated The Red Army
snippet.description:
In 1941, World War Two escalated into a global conflict of unprecedented scale. This documentary explores the pivotal moments of that fateful year, from the terrifying German U-boat wolf packs in the Battle Of The Atlantic and the dramatic sinking of the battleship Bismarck, to the brutal desert warfare of Erwin Rommel in North Africa. Most critically, we examine Operation Barbarossa—Hitler’s massive, genocidal invasion of the Soviet Union—and how the Russian colossus resisted the Nazi war machine just miles from Moscow, forever altering the course of world history.

snippet.title: The Edmund Fitzgerald: Did a Rogue Wave Sink the Great Lakes’ Invincible Freighter?
snippet.description:
Lake Superior’s deadliest storm claimed the "invincible" Edmund Fitzgerald. Discover the real reason she sank and the science behind the Great Lakes’ most famous shipwreck.

In this gripping deep dive, we investigate the tragic sinking of the Edmund Fitzgerald, the largest ship ever lost on the Great Lakes. Journey alongside divers and experts as they challenge the official story and explore the chilling power of Lake Superior's autumn storms, infamous for 30-foot waves and hurricane-force winds. The video reveals new forensic evidence, high-definition wreck footage, and dramatic survivor accounts from similar disasters, questioning whether human error or a catastrophic structural failure caused the ship to break apart on the surface.

Cutting-edge science and wave tank simulations show how rogue waves - once dismissed as sailor myths - may have been the final blow that doomed the Fitzgerald. Learn about the ship's controversial design, overloading practices, and the haunting aftermath for the families and communities left behind. If you're fascinated by shipwrecks, maritime mysteries, or the enduring legend of the Edmund Fitzgerald, this is a must-watch.

snippet.title: Doc Amores- An Explorer
snippet.description:
Dr. Alfonso "Docboy" Amores was a retired micro-surgeon and reconstructive surgery specialist when he came back to his home country after more than 20 years of living and working in the U.S.A. But he was not the kind of man who would be happy to whittle away his years in a rocking chair while watching the seasons pass.

He instead chose to do cave diving explorations. 

Unable to get satisfaction from breathing air or gas from a standard scuba set-up, he embarked to get educated in the use of a Closed-Circuit Rebreather (CCR). His weapon of choice was the Evolution CCR which he trained up to Trimix-level and of which he qualified as an IANTD Evolution CCR- Recreational Instructor.

In 2011 he made a dive with his unit to 100m/ 330ft.

Quite a feat considering he was already 65 years old at that time.

His efforts to go beyond certain barriers (like age) made people truly believe that he could do anything. Aside from being an extreme diver, he piloted his own plane (including a sea plane), skied on challenging ski slopes, organized noble medical missions, performed free surgery to indigents, educated children of the value of the coral reefs and created marine sanctuaries. Yes, he could do anything he set his mind on.

We will not dwell on how we lost him, we will instead remember a man who cared a lot for his family and for his fellowmen. We will remember a man who made sure he lived life to the fullest!

This video is a compilation of the dives we made in the Enchanted River on June 2011. We were denied entry by the cave at that time, but we were able to document a phenomenon previously unnoticed.

Verily, when certain doors are shut, other doors open to wonderful discoveries.

You will always live in our hearts, Doc!

snippet.description:
🚢 124 people dead in 20 seconds. A ship that capsized before sailing a single mile. The world's first filmed disaster that sparked a journalism ethics debate still raging today.

Welcome to Untraveled Mysteries!

There is a moment in the life of every vessel when years of planning and engineering culminate in a single, irreversible test. This video captures that critical instant: the ship construction process as the hull meets water, where physics becomes the ultimate judge. Witness the meticulous shipbuilding and the dramatic boat launch, highlighting the profound significance of these maritime events.

This is the complete, uncut history of 5 catastrophic ship launches that shocked the world—from the RMS Queen Mary's wave that caught 250,000 spectators off guard, to the SS Daphne that killed over a hundred workers in front of their families.


⚓ TIMESTAMPS:

04:35:12 - What I Learned: How These Disasters Changed Maritime Law


🎥 FEATURED DISASTERS:
- HMS Albion - Victorian London's darkest moment caught on film by 3 cameramen, sparking history's first journalism ethics debate
- SS Daphne - 124 workers, including fourteen and fifteen-year-old apprentice boys, killed instantly when anchors failed
- SS Great Eastern - Isambard Kingdom Brunel's cursed masterpiece that took 2 months to launch and bankrupted its backers
- SS Principessa Jolanda - Italy's largest luxury liner that lasted exactly 1 hour before capsizing in front of the King's daughter
- RMS Queen Mary - The Depression-era giant whose launch created a tidal wave (now one of America's most haunted locations)

🏴 Why These Stories Matter:
Every ship launch disaster led to new safety regulations:
- Daphne → Personnel limits during launches
- Albion → Crowd control requirements  
- Great Eastern → Stability calculation standards
- Jolanda → Launch-before-fitting protocols

These tragedies changed how ships are built forever.

Hopefield, Arkansas began as a Spanish outpost along the Mississippi River, meant as an outpost to stand in the way of the expansion of the newly formed United States of America. Then, it became French, then finally American. As it grew, it competed with the sprawling metropolis of Memphis, Tennessee.

snippet.title: 5 Hours of Titanic History
snippet.description:
RMS Titanic is history's most infamous ship - somehow the liner's story continues to grip us to this day. Few stories capture the imagination of the human mind as the tale of the RMS Titanic. It’s like a Greek tragedy - an epic that can resonate with everybody at any age and from any country around the globe.
